Skills.criterio: Ranked by the source repository's stars
Skills.criterioBody: We do not measure installs: nothing is installed through here, and an invented number would be the opposite of what this catalogue stands for. The stars belong to the repository the skill came from, fetched from the GitHub API. A heavily starred repository appears at most twice in a row and the rest is collapsed, or a single author would take the whole top.
Skills.hostedWhy: Permissive licence, copied with credit and a pinned commit.
Skills.atSourceWhy: No declared licence. Only the author may redistribute.

About.title: About the framework
About.dek: Compound Design is Danilo do Amaral's own framework for working with AI in design and code. AI-native: made for people and agents to read with the same care. The name is a thesis. Most work gets harder over time: each new thing negotiates with the old ones. Here it is the opposite. Each thing learned becomes an artefact that makes the next one easier — like compound interest.
About.purpose: A four-step method (plan, do, review, compound) and the artefacts it produces: data-backed articles, a catalogue of design-engineering skills with verified licences, and the CLI and MCP that put all of it in your agent's hands. AI-native means every part exists in two forms, one to read on screen and one for an agent to consume, and that the framework itself was built with the method it describes. All open: anyone can read, cite and reuse it.
About.authorBio: Danilo do Amaral is the author of Compound Design. A Design Engineer at Pitang Labs, five years into the intersection of AI, design and development. Postgraduate in UX & UI at EBAC and in UX Engineering at PUC Minas. He designs and builds prototypes, internal tools and agents, and writes about what he learns along the way.
About.how: Comment on the presentations, propose a skill for the catalogue or an article. Content marked as draft is open for review.
About.license: State of Prototyping Spring 2026 data belongs to UX Tools, under CC BY 4.0. The texts in the framework are by Danilo do Amaral.
About.philosophy: The loop has four steps: plan, do, review, compound. Anyone working with AI already does the first three. The fourth is what separates compounding from merely producing: what was learned becomes something reusable and findable — an article, a skill, a rule the system itself starts to check. Here, every fix that repeated became a check that breaks the build; every decision became a record; every good third-party skill entered the catalogue with credit. Most of the time goes to planning and reviewing, not typing. It is an open philosophy: the code, the decisions and the rules are in the repository for anyone to copy.

SkillsCli.title: CLI
SkillsCli.dek: Browse and fetch catalogue skills from your terminal. Reads the same registry as the page and the MCP server.
SkillsCli.noDeps: One JavaScript file, zero dependencies. It installs no framework to print a markdown file.
SkillsCli.attributionBody: get returns the markdown with the author and licence attached. For the {hosted} hosted ones the content comes from here; for the other {pointer} the command returns the card and the source address, because without a declared licence only the author may redistribute.

SkillsMcp.title: MCP
SkillsMcp.dek: Connect agents to the catalogue over Model Context Protocol. The server exposes the same registry as the CLI.
SkillsMcp.connectBody: HTTP transport, no authentication. In Claude Code, add this to your MCP configuration file:
SkillsMcp.listSkills: Lists the skills, in pages of 40. Filters by free text and by topic, and takes limit and offset. Each item carries author and licence, not just name and description.
SkillsMcp.getSkill: Fetches a skill's markdown by name, slug or author/slug. Use name: "start" for the routing skill. When a name exists under more than one author, it returns the options instead of choosing for you.
SkillsMcp.provenanceBody: The {hosted} hosted ones come back with the text and the attribution. The other {pointer} come back with the card and the source address: without a declared licence, serving the text would mean redistributing what is not ours.
SkillsMcp.listTopics: The catalogue's topics, with how many skills each holds. Use it before listing: there are hundreds of entries, and picking a topic keeps the agent's context from filling up for nothing.
SkillsMcp.pagingBody: The whole catalogue in one response came to 157 KB, roughly 40,000 tokens landing in the context of an agent that only wanted to know what exists. Listings come in pages of 40 and say how much was left out, with the offset for the next. Nothing is trimmed in silence.
SkillsMcp.limitsBody: No authentication, with a ceiling of 120 calls per minute per address. A normal session makes about a dozen; the ceiling is there to catch an agent stuck in a loop.
